title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range

segments.text: Hi everyone, I'm Matt Rigon and I'm a
financial planner at Range. I want to
show you how our financial planners
ended up writing the agents that we use
every day and none of us the financial
planners for that matter write code.
This is the build guide. How we did it
step by step so you can take it back to
your own teams, companies, etc. So, a
quick bit about me because it matters
for how you'll hear this talk. I'm not
an engineer. I'm a certified financial
planner and I spend my days with clients
talking about cash flow, taxes,
insurance, retirement, estate, you name
it. I also lead the AI adoption for the
planning team at Range, which is an
all-in-one wealth management company.
Most agent talks you'll hear come from
the people who built the platform. This
talk comes from someone on the other
side, the people you hand the platform
to. We work in a regulated business. The
output is financial advice to real
clients. And the review step is not
optional. So, this isn't a vendor pitch.
It's a method and it's what actually
worked for us.
We started where everyone starts AI as a
chatbot. I'd write a client message,
paste it in, and ask it to make it a
little clearer or friendlier. And that
was useful. It saved me a few minutes
here and there, but I was still doing
all of the work manually. I was just
doing it a little bit faster. The change
that actually mattered came later.
Here's what we figured out. A planner's
constraint was never typing speed, for
example. It's that we can only be in one
place at a time. If I'm on a call with a
client, I'm not building someone else's
plan. Writing faster doesn't fix that
problem. What fixes it is work that
happens while I'm somewhere else. So,
here's what a day looks like now. I'm on
a call with one client. At the same
time, an agent is drafting a full cash
flow analysis or an insurance analysis
for a different client. When the call
ends, I open that draft. I fully review
it, adjust what needs to be adjusted,
and send the client their
recommendations. I want to be really
clear about that last step. The agent
doesn't send anything. A planner reviews
every single recommendation before a
client sees it. What changed is that the
first draft no longer needs me sitting
in front of it. Getting there took a lot
more than a good prompt. However, two
things had to be true. First, the agent
has to work where the work lives, not in
a separate chat window I'm copying and
pasting it into. Second, it has to know
how we do it, not how financial planning
works in general. The model already
knows that, but the agent needs to know
how range does it. What we look at
first, what we always flag, how we
phrase a specific recommendation. That
combination is what a skill is. Our
firm's way of doing one specific piece
of work written down so an agent can
follow it.
The bulk of this talk
is how you build one. Five steps. Pick,
teach, pack, test, and then ship. None
of them require writing code. Every one
of them requires knowing the work really
well, which is exactly why the people
doing the work should also be the ones
building it.
Step one, pick a workflow you repeat.
Your initial instinct is to go for the
flashiest work, whatever's taking the
most amount of time and the most
complex. Don't pick something you do
every week where you already know what
good looks like, where you can spot a
bad draft at a glance. Additionally, we
recommend choosing some of the least
complex workflows to start, but some
that require the most manual work. For
us, that meant things like cash flow
analysis and insurance reviews. Just for
us here at range, that required the most
manual work. And if you can't judge the
output quickly, you can't test it and
you can't trust it. So look for two
things. You do it often and you know how
to judge it.
Step two, show it several real cases for
previous plans you've delivered. Take
several actual client cases and walk
through the work start to finish. And as
you do it, narrate your judgment out
loud. Not just next I open the pastub,
why you're opening it, what you're
looking for, what would make you stop
and ask a question. That narration is
the whole game. The steps are easy to
write down. The judgment is what makes
it your firm's work instead of generic
advice.
Step three, pack it into a skill. A
skill isn't just a lip a list of steps.
Two things matter most. The questions it
must ask before it starts. What does it
need to know? What should it confirm
with me instead of simply guessing? And
the limits it must respect. What it
never does on its own. In our world, the
big one is that it never sends anything
to a client. It drafts and then a
planner decides if it gets sent or needs
to be adjusted. If you only write the
steps, you get something that simply
just runs on its own. If you write the
questions and set the limits, you can
get something you can trust. Think of a
skill as a recipe. Once Claude knows how
to do the skill, it will repeat your
process on command.
Step number four, run it five or 10
times on real cases before anyone else
sees it. This is the step everyone wants
to skip. Every run teaches you something
the skill didn't know yet. An edge case,
a question it should have asked, a spot
where it sounded confident and was
wrong. You need to fix it, save the
skill, and run it again and again and
again. Five to 10 runs sounds like a
lot, but it's a lot less work than
cleaning up after you hand a halfbaked
skill to 15, 20, 100 people in your
team.
Step five, ship it with an owner and a
reviewer. The owner keeps it current.
Our processes change, tax rules change,
and a skill that was right in March can
be wrong by December. The reviewer
checks it before the team relies on it.
And it's someone other than the author.
Same as a plan, you don't grade your own
work. Once other people depend on a
skill, somebody has to be accountable
for it. That's the difference between a
clever personal shortcut and something a
team can build on. So, where are we at
currently? Six months in, we have 24
skills across the company and 17 of them
are in planning. And here's the part I
didn't expect. It spread to sales,
product, marketing, all without a
mandate. Nobody sent a memo. People saw
what the planners were doing and started
building their own agents.
Every one of those skills was written
and is maintained by planners,
marketers, and salespeople, not
developers or engineers.
A couple of things changed once subject
matter experts started building for
their own niche. The skills got a lot
more specific. The person who knows
insurance, for example, best builds the
insurance skill. The person who best
knows tax, tax code, tax law should be
building the tax one. and a review came
naturally. We already review each
other's plans and that's just how
planning works. So now we review each
other's skills in that same way. It's
the same habit, just a new thing to
review.
So why does this matter right now?
Because the bottleneck has moved.
Whether a model can draft a cash flow
analysis, that question's already been
settled. It can. What's not settled? Who
writes down how your firm does it? who
tests it before it ships, who owns it
once 15 other people depend on it. If
you're being asked to push agents out
past the engineering org, you're about
to hit these exact questions. There
isn't much field data on this yet, but
this is how we've done it here at Range.
So, that's it. Thank you so much for
listening to this talk. I'm Matt Rigon
from Range and you can reach me for at
mattrange.com.
Have a great day.
